title: The lowest of all
hook: whoever knows himself lowest of all is counted highest (Sukhmani 12)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the proud fall, and your line: pride falls. Did you leave the flattering part out of a story? Today the same ashtpadi flips the ladder upside down. Day four hundred eighty-four.

Sikh tradition tells of an old man who carried water. Every morning before dawn, for years, he walked to the river, filled a pitcher, and brought it back for his teacher, Guru Angad, to bathe. One dark, stormy morning he tripped near a weaver's house and fell into the pit where the loom stood. The weaver's wife heard the noise and said, more or less: that's only Amru, the man with no home, who wanders around after his guru. A nobody. That nobody was the man who became the third Guru, Guru Amar Das. Today Sukhmani gives the rule his life was following.
screen: `AN OLD MAN CARRIES WATER.` → `HE FALLS. ONLY AMRU, A NOBODY.` → `THE NOBODY BECOMES THE THIRD GURU.`

segments.voice: Later in the twelfth ashtpadi, after the prides have been named, Guru Arjan turns the ladder over. Aapas kau jo jaanai neechaa, sou ganeeai sabh te oochaa. Whoever knows himself to be low is counted the highest of all. Two words carry the line. Neechaa: low, beneath. Oochaa: high, above. They're ordinary Punjabi, words for a shelf or a hill. And the verb in the middle matters: ganeeai, is counted, is reckoned. The line doesn't say the humble person feels high, or gets promoted at work. It says that in the real reckoning, God's count, the order is reversed. The next line deepens it: the one whose mind becomes the dust of all recognizes the Name in every heart. That's the reason the low place works. When you're not looking down on anyone, you can finally see what's in them. Back to the story. Tradition says when Guru Angad heard what the weaver's wife had called Amar Das, the homeless one, he answered by calling him the home of the homeless. The insult turned into a title. Tradition says Amar Das was already an old man when he became Guru, and that he asked everyone who came to see him, even, in the story, the emperor Akbar, to eat first in the langar, in the same rows as everyone else. The lowest seat, made into the door. So this isn't a trick for getting ahead, being humble now to be on top later. The stanza is describing how things are already counted. We just can't see the scoreboard.
screen: `NEECHAA: LOW. OOCHAA: HIGH.` · `COUNTED, NOT FELT.` · `THE DUST OF ALL SEES EVERY HEART.` · `HOME OF THE HOMELESS.` · then, large: `LOWEST IS HIGHEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve someone quietly, in your mind first. Bring to mind one person whose day you could make easier, a roommate, a coworker, someone at home. Picture one small thing you could do for them that they may never notice: the dishes, a refilled water jug, a door held. Picture yourself doing it and walking away without a word. Let that feel like enough. Then, if it's possible today, do it. The bell holds the time.
The lowest of all. Aapas kau jo jaanai neechaa: whoever knows himself low is counted highest, the way an old water carrier became the third Guru.
Your line: lowest is highest. Do one helpful thing today that nobody will thank you for, and don't mention it. Day four hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Amar Das's years of carrying water for Guru Angad as a model of seva, and in gurdwaras today volunteers wash dishes, sweep and mind shoes, often without anyone knowing their names.

fork.setup: you're Guru Angad. someone has mocked your devoted student as a homeless nobody. what do you say?
options: call him the home of the homeless.
fork.reveal: tradition says he called Amar Das the home of the homeless: the insult became a title.

original.note: Gurmukhi: neechaa, low; paired in the line with oochaa, high.

trapdoor: what you thought: be humble now so you can be on top later.
what it means: in the real reckoning the order is already reversed; the low place lets you see the Name in every heart.
what a scholar hears: the verb is ganeeai, is reckoned, a word of counting and accounts, so the line is about how God keeps score.

notes: aapas kau jo jaanai neechaa, sou ganeeai sabh te oochaa and jaa kaa man hoi sagal kee reenaa: confirm both lines sit at the end of ashtpadi 12 stanza 1 (Ang 278) and the transliteration.
The weaver's pit story, nithaavaan, and Guru Angad's reply (nithaaviaan da thaan, nimaaniaan da maan): tradition, not Gurbani; confirm wording and sources.
Guru Amar Das's age at becoming Guru (traditionally about 73) and the 'pehle pangat, peechhe sangat' langar tradition including Emperor Akbar: confirm.
